1.goal: To open the lesson on a situation she already knows from work, and to tell her what the lesson ends with.
1.interaction: T–S, spoken. One open question; Portuguese is fine at this point.
run: Tell her what the lesson ends with, in one sentence: she compares two documents and briefs her coordinator on where they disagree.
Ask the question on screen and take one answer.
exact: What today is: “Today you read a lesson plan and a course syllabus. Then you tell your coordinator where they disagree.”
If she answers in general terms: “Think of one time. Which two documents were they?”
1.expected: One episode from her own work, named in a sentence or two. A complete answer looks like “Last month, the course description and the coursebook map for the B2 group. They had different units.” — the two documents and what did not match.
1.support: If nothing comes to mind, name two kinds of pair and let her pick one: a plan and a syllabus, or a course description and what is actually taught.
1.challenge: Ask what she did once she found the mismatch: who she told, and in what order.
1.monitoring: Whether she reaches for a real episode or a general one. The real one gives the briefing on screen 9 something to draw on.
1.evidence: The example she gives, in her words.
1.transition: Move on when she has given one concrete example.

2.goal: To establish who is asking, what the coordinator needs, and what she should leave the meeting with.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the brief on screen together.
run: Read the brief with her.
Ask the question on screen and let her answer in one sentence.
2.expected: Something close to “She needs to know where the two documents disagree and what has to be decided, and by whom.” The brief gives both parts in the last two lines; the three differences are not named here, and the first reading is where they appear.
2.support: If she answers with what the documents say, point at “What you want by the end” and read it with her.
2.challenge: Ask what she would want to know before briefing someone who is going straight into another meeting.
2.monitoring: Whether she states the task from the brief or starts guessing the content of the documents.
2.evidence: Whether she can say the task in one sentence without rereading the brief.
2.transition: Move on when she has said, in one sentence, what the coordinator needs.

3.goal: To have her commit to three guesses before she reads, so the first reading has something to confirm.
3.interaction: T–S, guessing out loud. Nothing is confirmed or corrected here.
run: Read the three questions with her.
Take one answer on each. Leave them unconfirmed: the documents on the next screen settle them.
Note her three answers where she can see them. She checks them herself on the next screen.
exact: Before moving on: “Those are your guesses. Now we read and see.”
3.expected: There is no answer key on this screen: the three questions are open. For your reference, what the documents will show: they disagree on the hours, on who corrects the written work and on the assessment week; the syllabus is the promise to people outside the school; and the plan is the one that is usually changed.
3.support: If she answers about documents in general, ask her to answer about a plan and a syllabus for one course in her own school.
3.challenge: Ask which of her three guesses she would bet on, and why.
3.monitoring: Whether she risks a guess or waits to be told.
3.evidence: Her three guesses, kept for screen 4.
3.transition: Move on when all three questions have an answer, right or wrong.

4.goal: To read each document once for what it is, before comparing what they say.
run: Give her about three minutes for the two documents.
Ask the question on screen.
Then ask which of her guesses from screen 3 the documents confirm.
4.expected: The lesson plan is for one unit and is written by a teacher for their own teaching; it can be adjusted. The syllabus is for the whole semester and states what the course commits to, so it is written for people outside the classroom: the coordination, the next teacher, the students. The line that shows it: “This syllabus states what the course commits to.”
4.support: Ask who each document was written for. That question does most of the work.
4.challenge: Ask which of the two would be harder to change, and who would have to agree.
4.monitoring: Whether she reads for what each document is, or starts collecting differences straight away. If she names a difference, note it for screen 5.
4.evidence: The words she uses for the difference between the two documents. They come back in the briefing.
4.transition: Move on when she has said what each document is for.

5.goal: To attribute each of six statements to the document that supports it, going back to the line instead of answering from memory.
5.interaction: S alone on the activity, then T–S to check.
run: Let her place all six on her own and press Check when she has finished. The button checks the whole activity at once.
Then go through the six out loud. On each, ask her to open the documents with the button on screen and read the line that decides it.
Spend the time that is left on the statement that neither document supports.
exact: On each statement: “Which line says that? Read it to me.”
On the listening task: “The syllabus does not mention the task. Does that mean it was removed?”
5.expected: The course syllabus: “Going over the allocated hours needs approval from above.” (no unit may run beyond its allocation without approval from the coordination) · “Feedback on the written work comes back within one week.” The lesson plan: “Someone other than the teacher corrects the report first.” (corrected by a classmate) · “The students hear a recording of a meeting.” (the listening task in session 4). Both of them: “Unit 7 ends with a piece of written work.” Neither of them: “The listening task was removed from the course.” — the syllabus does not mention the task, and it says it does not list every task a teacher may use.
5.support: If she answers from memory, open the documents and ask her to find the line before she chooses.
5.challenge: Ask which of the three real differences the coordinator would have to settle first, and why.
5.monitoring: Whether she goes back to the document or answers from memory. If she calls the listening task a fourth difference, it is the discovery of screens 6 and 7 arriving early.
5.evidence: Whether she returned to the documents, and on which statements.
5.transition: Move on when the six are placed and the listening task has been discussed.

6.goal: To have her notice that three different things end up in the same kind of sentence: what a document says, what she concluded, and what she recommends.
6.interaction: S alone on the activity, then T–S.
run: Let her classify the six sentences and press Check.
Go through them out loud. On each one in the document, ask where it is written.
Leave the test for the next screen: here she only sorts.
6.expected: It is in the document: “The syllabus allocates 20 hours to Unit 7.” · “The plan has the assessment one week earlier than the syllabus.” · “The syllabus does not claim to list every task.” I concluded it: “The course was shortened at some point.” · “Peer correction was put in to save the teacher time.” It is what I think we should do: “We should fix the assessment week before the group starts.”
6.support: On each sentence, ask whether the words are written in one of the documents.
6.challenge: Ask her to turn the recommendation into a conclusion, and to say what changes.
6.monitoring: Whether she separates the two conclusions from the sentences that are written in the documents. She is precise about this in Portuguese; what may be missing is the English that marks it.
6.evidence: Which sentences she placed in the document when they were conclusions.
6.transition: Move on when the six are sorted.

7.goal: To have her find the test that separates a conclusion from what a document says, and hear the English that marks each one.
run: Read the question and the two sentences on screen with her.
Let her answer before you open the button.
Open the test and read it with her. Then ask her for one sentence of each kind about the two documents.
exact: If she does not see it: “Imagine the coordinator has the syllabus in front of her. Can she disagree with the first sentence? And with the second?”
Asking for examples: “Give me one sentence that is in the plan, and one that is your reading.”
7.expected: Someone with the documents could not disagree with “The syllabus allocates 20 hours to Unit 7.”, but could disagree with “The course was shortened at some point.”, because no document says it. From the reveal: in the document — “The syllabus says twenty hours.”; a conclusion — “My reading is that the course was shortened.”; a recommendation — “I would fix the week before the group starts.”
7.support: Cover the second sentence, ask about the first only, then uncover it.
7.challenge: Ask her for another way to mark a conclusion besides “My reading is that…”.
7.monitoring: Whether she finds the test before the reveal, and whether her own examples mark the conclusion.
7.evidence: Her own examples, in her words.
7.transition: Move on when the test has been read and she has given one sentence of each kind.

8.goal: To say the three differences out loud with the source at the start of the sentence, before the briefing.
8.interaction: T–S, spoken, one difference at a time.
run: Play the five sentences once, and ask her where the source is in each one.
Ask for the three differences one at a time: the hours, who corrects the written work, the assessment week.
When the source comes at the end, ask her to say the sentence again with the source first.
Open the model briefing after she has said all three, and ask where the sources are in it.
exact: Asking for the first one: “The hours. Tell me, and start with the document.”
Rebuilding a late source: “Say that again, and start with where it comes from: The syllabus says…”
8.expected: Three sentences with the source at the start, for example “The syllabus says twenty hours, and the plan has eighteen.”, “These two do not line up on who corrects the writing: the syllabus says the teacher, the plan says a classmate.” and “According to the plan, the assessment is in week seven; the syllabus puts it in week eight.” Any form that puts the source with the claim is correct, including forms that are not on the screen.
8.support: If the source keeps arriving after the fact — “It is twenty hours… that is the syllabus” — say the first three words of the sentence and let her finish it.
8.challenge: Ask for the same three with a different opening each time.
8.monitoring: Where the source lands in each sentence.
8.evidence: How many of the three carried the source at the start without help.
8.transition: Move on when the three differences have been said with the source in the sentence.

9.goal: To brief the coordinator on the three differences, attributing each claim as she makes it and marking her own reading, with the sentence starters closed.
9.interaction: Role-play. You are the coordinator; she briefs you.
run: Read the task and the list on screen with her.
Let her run until she has given at least two differences. Then interrupt once, with the question below, and let her come back to where she was.
The sentence starters stay closed. Open them only if she stops, let her look, and close them again.
Leave corrections for screen 11. Write down one sentence as she said it.
exact: The interruption: “Sorry, which of the two is the one we promised the students?”
9.expected: Five things in one turn, in the order of the list: what the two documents are; the three differences — the hours (20 in the syllabus, 18 in the plan), who corrects the written work (the teacher in the syllabus, a classmate in the plan) and the assessment week (week 8 in the syllabus, week 7 in the plan), each with its document; one part marked as her reading; an answer to the interruption (the syllabus is the one promised to the students); and what has to be decided, and by whom.
9.support: If she stops, point at the next item on the list before you open the starters.
9.challenge: Ask her to say which difference matters most for the group starting next month.
9.monitoring: Where the source lands in each sentence, and whether her reading is still marked after the interruption.
9.evidence: One sentence of the briefing, written word for word. It goes into the boards on screen 11.
9.transition: Move on when she has given the three differences and said what has to be decided.

10.goal: To keep the conversation going after the prepared briefing: answer two real questions from the coordinator, and ask one back.
10.interaction: T–S, unscripted. You are still the coordinator.
run: Ask the two questions below, one at a time.
After each answer, wait. Give her time to add the source or to mark her reading.
Then ask her to put one question to you about the decision, and answer it.
exact: Question 1: “The plan has fewer hours than the syllabus. Is that a problem, or only a difference?”
Question 2: “Who should I talk to first, the teacher who wrote the plan or the head of studies?”
Handing the turn over: “Is there anything you need from me?”
10.expected: Two answers that say where they come from, and one question from her. On the first question: the syllabus only forbids running beyond the allocation, so eighteen hours is not against it — a complete answer marks the rest as her reading, for example “The syllabus only says a unit cannot go over its hours. My reading is that the students would lose two hours they were promised.” On the second there is no answer in the documents, so any answer marked as her recommendation is correct (“I would talk to the teacher first”). Her question can be as small as “Do you want me to put this in writing?”.
10.support: If she answers without a source, ask “Is that in one of the documents?” and wait.
10.challenge: Push back once: “But the syllabus says twenty. Eighteen breaks that promise.” Let her answer from the line.
10.monitoring: Whether she marks what is her reading when the question has no answer in the documents.
10.evidence: Whether she marked her reading without being asked, and whether she asked a question of her own.
10.transition: Move on when she has answered the two questions and asked one.

11.goal: To give one piece of feedback she can use, and to run the briefing again for a listener who disagrees.
11.interaction: T–S, filling the boards together, then the replay.
run: Write one thing that worked and one point to improve in the boards on screen.
Write the sentence you noted on screen 9 as she said it, and build a clearer version with her in the fourth box.
Open the replay. You now play the teacher who wrote the plan, and you think the plan is right. She gives the three differences again.
exact: Opening the replay: “I wrote that plan, and I think it works. What exactly is the problem?”
11.expected: The same three differences, each still attributed to its document, told to someone who defends the plan. A complete second version sounds like “I see why you gave it to a classmate, but the syllabus says the teacher corrects the written work.” — the other person's point acknowledged, and the source kept.
11.support: Point at the line on screen and let her use it word for word the first time.
11.challenge: Defend the plan once more after her first difference, and let her keep the source in her answer.
11.monitoring: Whether the sources stay in the sentences when the listener disagrees.
11.evidence: Whether the point to improve from the boards appeared in the replay.
11.transition: Move on when the replay has been said.

12.goal: To close on what was worked on, let her say how confident she feels, and leave the homework said out loud.
12.interaction: T–S, going through the recap and the confidence scale together.
run: Go through the recap list with her and tick what was done.
Let her fill the confidence scale herself.
Read the three lines on the right and say the homework out loud.
exact: The homework, said out loud: “This week, when you tell someone what a document says, start the sentence with the document.”
12.expected: The recap has seven lines, and all seven were done if the lesson ran to the end: reading the two documents against each other, telling what a document states from what she concluded, finding the line that supports a statement, putting the source in the sentence, marking a conclusion as hers, answering an interruption and coming back, and answering the coordinator's questions after the briefing. The confidence scale is hers, and it may come out lower than what you saw.
12.support: If she marks everything low, name one sentence she said today with the source at the start.
12.challenge: Ask which of today's phrases she would use first in a meeting she has this week.
12.monitoring: Whether her self-assessment matches what you observed. The gap is worth noting.
12.evidence: Her confidence marks, and anything she said about the pre-class.
12.transition: End here. The next lesson is a call with three people talking about a coursebook.
